## Raptors Using a Solar Photovoltaic Facility in Southern Spain

## Adrián Martín-Taboada ,[1,2] Pablo García-Quevedo ,[1] Francisco Díaz-Ruiz ,[3] Jesús Duarte ,[4] Raimundo Real ,[2] Miguel Senghor Machado Karekezi ,[1] and Miguel A. Farfán 2

1BioGea Consultores, C/Navarro Ledesma 243, 29010 Málaga, Spain

2Biogeography, Diversity and Conservation Research Team, Departamento de Biología Animal, Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad de Málaga, E-29071, Spain

3Conservation Biology Research Group, Departamento de Anatomía, Biología Celular y Zoología, Universidad de Extremadura, 06006 Badajoz, Spain 4Ofitecma Marbella S.L., Av. Ramón y Cajal 17, 29601 Marbella, Spain

ABSTRACT.—The global energy crisis triggered by the Russian invasion of Ukraine led to an unprecedented increase in the use of renewable energies. According to the International Energy Agency, the solar photovoltaic (PV) energy will be the energy source with the largest installed electricity capacity in the world by 2027. However, the lack of knowledge of its medium- and long-term impact on wildlife is concerning. In this study, we monitored the occurrence of raptors at a PV facility located in Andalusia, Spain, during the first two and a half years of operation. We recorded the presence of six species at the PV facility. The most frequent were the Eurasian Buzzard (Buteo buteo) and the Eurasian Kestrel (Falco tinnunculus), which were observed in 88.9% of the samplings, followed by the Black Kite (Milvus migrans) at 83.3% and the Red Kite (Milvus milvus) at 55.6%. The least frequent were the Booted Eagle (Hieraaetus pennatus) and the Little Owl (Athene noctua), which were observed in 16.7% and 5.6% of the samplings, respectively. The most frequent raptor behaviors were perching (38.1%) and flying (37.7%), followed by hunting (14.8%), circling (9.1%), and breeding and territorial displays (0.3%). The results are notable due to the observed use by the raptors, which, at least in our study, shows the compatibility between this type of energy production infrastructure and raptor occurrence. Nevertheless, the absence of data on the pre-existing conditions before the establishment of the solar PV facility hinders our ability to determine the impact of these infrastructures on raptor communities.

KEY WORDS: Andalusia; behavior; conservation; human-wildlife conflicts; photovoltaic solar energy; renewable energy.

## USO POR RAPACES DE UNA INSTALACIÓN FOTOVOLTAICA EN EL SUR DE ESPAÑA

RESUMEN.—La crisis energética mundial desencadenada por la invasión de Rusia en Ucrania provocó un aumento sin precedentes en el uso de energías renovables. Según la Agencia Internacional de la Energía, para 2027 la energía solar fotovoltaica (FV) será la fuente de energía con mayor capacidad eléctrica instalada en el mundo. Sin embargo, el desconocimiento de su impacto en la fauna silvestre a medio y largo plazo es preocupante. En este estudio se monitoreó la ocurrencia de aves rapaces en una planta solar FV, ubicada en Andalucía, España, durante los dos primeros años y medio de funcionamiento. Se registraron seis especies dentro de la instalación solar FV. Las más frecuentes fueron Buteo buteo y Falco tinnunculus, observadas en el 88,9% de los muestreos, seguidas de Milvus migrans con un 83,3% y Milvus milvus con un 55,6%. Las menos frecuentes fueron Hieraaetus pennatus y Athene noctua, observadas en el 16,7% y 5,6% de los muestreos, respectivamente. Los comportamientos observados con mayor frecuencia dentro de la instalación solar FV fueron: posado (38,1%) y vuelos direccionales

## INTRODUCTION

In recent decades, the use of renewable energy has been increasing as an alternative to fossil fuelbased technologies to reduce the emission of harmful pollutants into the atmosphere and mitigate the adverse effects of carbon dioxide on the climate (Shapifee and Topal 2009, Allison et al. 2014). The recent global energy crisis triggered by the Russian invasion to Ukraine has led to an unprecedented increase in renewable energy demand. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), renewable energies were projected to become the primary source of global electricity generation by 2025, and solar photovoltaic (PV) will be the energy source with the world’s largest installed electricity capacity of approximately 2350 GW by 2027 (IEA 2023). Spain is among the seven European countries where the installed capacity of renewable energies, mainly solar PV, will grow the most in the coming years. The IEA (2023) forecasts that Spain will almost double its installed renewable electricity capacity by 2027, increasing the current capacity by 58 GW (46.6% from solar PV).

The expansion of solar PV facilities, along with the short-term growth forecast of this type of infrastructure and the limited scientific knowledge of its medium- and long-term impact on wildlife, are cause of concern. Solar PV facilities could affect wildlife through habitat destruction and fragmentation, barrier effects, and direct mortality (Walston et al. 2016, Agha et al. 2020, Kosciuch et al. 2020, Tinsley et al. 2023), although scientific literature is still scarce. Another understudied aspect is the behavioral response of wildlife to solar PV facilities, as behavioral changes are often the first response of animals to environmental changes and are noticeable indications of detrimental effects (Dimitri and Longland 2018).

Making the development of solar PV energy compatible with wildlife conservation requires further research into the behavioral responses of wildlife to this type of infrastructure. This issue has been addressed in several countries such as Egypt, Pakistan, South Africa, France, Germany, and Spain,

among others, or in certain states in the United States. Specifically, in Spain, the current environmental legislation requires that solar PV facilities monitor wildlife during the operation phase and follow up on the corrective and compensatory measures implemented to minimize the possible impact of this type of infrastructure on wildlife (Ministerio para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico 2022). In this study, we report our findings of wildlife monitoring during the first 2.5 yr of the operation of a solar PV facility in southern Spain to analyze the occurrence and behavior of raptors inside the facility. We expect that the presence of the solar PV facility alters the environment in a manner that deters raptors from using it (Smith and Dwyer 2016). We also discuss management and conservation implications related to our findings.

## METHODS

Study Area. Our study was conducted at a 150MW, 299-ha solar PV facility located in Seville Province, Andalusia (southern Spain). The solar panels are mounted at a fixed tilt angle, with uniform inter-row spacing consistently maintained across the entire installation. The climate is warm and temperate, with an average annual temperature of 18.8[] C, and mean annual rainfall of 483 mm. August is the warmest month with an average of 28.4[] C, while January is the coldest month with temperatures averaging 10.3[] C. The driest months are July and August with an average rainfall of 2 mm, and the most humid month is December with an average of 77 mm of rainfall (Climate Data 2023).

The facility is located in a predominantly flat region with gentle undulations mainly occupied by crops with scattered patches of natural vegetation. Agricultural land consists mainly of arable cereal crops and, to a lesser extent, olive trees (Olea europaea). The natural vegetation includes scattered stone pine (Pinus pinea) and shrub species, such as the purple Jerusalem sage (Phlomis purpurea), Mediterranean dwarf palm (Chamaerops humilis), rough bindweed (Smilax aspera), mastic (Pistacia lentiscus), kermes oak (Quercus coccifera), and tamarisk (Tamarix

A perimeter fence surrounds the facility. Human activity inside the facility is very limited and is restricted to maintenance work, wildlife monitoring and, outside of the bird-breeding season, vegetation control by sheep grazing.

Raptor Monitoring. From July 2022 to December 2024, coinciding with the first 2.5 yr of operation of the solar PV facility, two observers equipped with 8 3 42 binoculars and a 703 telescope recorded the occurrence and behavior of the raptors inside the solar PV facility. Observers conducted 18 samplings inside the solar PV facility. We used two methodologies: (1) observing and listening from two fixed points with a 360-degree visibility of the solar PV installation, and (2) walking a 2150-m fixed linear transect (Tellería 1986, Bibby et al. 2000). Sam– plings took 3 5 hr, depending on the time required to complete the transect and to conduct observations at the sampling points, and were performed in the morning from dawn until 1400 H and under favorable weather conditions (i.e., without rain or strong winds and with clear visibility). The collected information was incorporated into a database specifically designed for subsequent analysis.

Based on Farfán et al. (2009), we collected the following information during samplings: (1) number of observations per species. Each observation includes sightings of individuals or groups of birds; and (2) total number of individuals observed per species. We estimated the frequency of raptor occurrence as the number of samplings in which each species was observed (expressed in %). We estimated the relative abundance for each species based on the number of observations and the number of individuals recorded. In both cases, we collected data on species that were observed only

within the solar PV facility. In addition, we recorded the birds’ behavior classified into the following categories: (a) perching: perched or resting on a structure of the solar PV facility (i.e., photovoltaic plate, poles, perimeter fence, or transformers); (b) circling: thermal lifting to gain altitude over the solar PV facility; (c) hunting: direct observations of hunting and hunting behaviors (i.e., flights in search of prey, such as hovering); (d) flying: directional flights (not soaring on a thermal) over the solar PV facility; (e) breeding and territorial displays: behavior exhibited by raptors during courtship and to defend and protect a specific area against other individuals of the same or different species.

We used the chi-square test to determine whether the frequency of observed behaviors within the solar PV facility differed significantly from the values expected randomly (Sokal and Rohlf 1981).

Raptor Mortality. During the study period, we conducted systematic surveys (totaling 54 hr) to evaluate raptor mortality from collisions with solar panels, support structures, and the perimeter fence of the solar PV facility. We systematically inspected the perimeter fence and the rows of solar modules from the internal service roads that traverse the solar PV facility.

## RESULTS

We observed six raptor species in all the samplings inside the solar PV facility. We recorded 318 observations, including 2082 individual records (Table 1). The most frequent species were the Eurasian Buzzard (Buteo buteo) and the Eurasian Kestrel (Falco tinnunculus), followed by the Black Kite (Milvus migrans) and the Red Kite (Milvus milvus). The least frequent were the Booted Eagle (Hieraaetus pennatus) and the Little Owl (Athene noctua). Based on the number of observations and individuals, the

most abundant species was the Black Kite. This was followed by the Red Kite, Eurasian Buzzard and the Eurasian Kestrel. The species with fewest observations were the Little Owl and Booted Eagle.

Overall, the most frequently observed behaviors inside the solar PV facility were perching (121 observations, 38.1%) and flying (120 observations, 37.7%), followed by hunting (47 observations, 14.8%), circling (29 observations, 9.1%), and finally breeding and territorial displays (one observation, 0.3%). We found significant differences between the observed proportion of the different behaviors (chi-square 1⁄4 186.591, df 1⁄4 4, P , 0.001; Fig. 1). The frequency of observed behaviors varied among species. The Eurasian Buzzard, the Eurasia Kestrel, the Black Kite, and the Red Kite were observed mostly perching and flying, and the differences compared to the rest of behaviors considered were statistically significant (Eurasian Buzzard: chisquare 1⁄4 49.346, df 1⁄4 4, P , 0.01; Eurasian Kestrel: chi-square 1⁄4 42.293, df 1⁄4 4, P , 0.01; Black Kite: chisquare 1⁄4 64.657, df 1⁄4 4, P , 0.01; Red Kite: chi-square 1⁄4 45.579, df 1⁄4 4, P , 0.01). In the case of the Little Owl, the two individuals were recorded perching, while for the Booted Eagle, four individuals were observed displaying different behaviors. On one occasion, on 11 April 2023, we observed an adult Eurasian Buzzard capture a wild rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus).

During the entire study, we found no dead or injured raptors in the solar PV facility.

## DISCUSSION

Currently, the destruction, degradation, and fragmentation of large areas of natural habitats

have been the main concerns associated with the development of solar PV facilities, especially when threatened birds with specific habitat requirements like steppe birds or bird of prey, could be affected. Scientific literature on this topic discusses the potential effects on wildlife associated with solar facilities, but papers supported by empirical evidence are still scarce (Tsoutsos et al. 2005, Chock et al. 2020, Gómez-Catasús et al. 2024).

We found that there are raptor species using the different structures of our study solar PV facility as roosting and resting areas, as hunting territories and, in the case of soaring species, as areas for gaining altitude. We found five raptor species hunting inside the solar PV facility. One species was the Red Kite, which is classified as endangered according to the Spanish Catalogue of Threatened Species (Boletín Oficial del Estado 2011). The hunting frequency observed in our study could be underestimated due to the low probability of detecting such events. However, perching behavior, the most frequent of the behaviors we observed, may often be associated with hunting by raptors.

The frequency and abundance observed in our study varied among species. The less frequent species were the Booted Eagle and Little Owl. For the Booted Eagle, this could be justified because the solar PV facility is located in a flat open area, a different habitat from the forest environments in which the Booted Eagle is primarily found (Barrientos and Arroyo 2014). The Little Owl may be more difficult to detect due to its predominantly nocturnal habits, an aspect that has not been addressed in the present study, and also its propensity to fly at a

very low altitude between the lines of solar modules (A. Martín-Taboada unpubl. data). The abundance of both kite species, especially Black Kites, may be affected by the presence of an urban solid waste treatment center in the vicinity and by the tolerance these species show toward human presence (Blanco 1997, Radi et al. 2020).

Raptors’ presence and use of the solar PV facility may be promoted by the following: (1) the minimal human activity inside the solar PV facility, which is limited to maintenance work by technicians and wildlife monitoring; (2) the regular presence of potential prey species, such as the Red-legged Partridge (Alectoris rufa), wild rabbit, Iberian hare (Lepus granatensis), and several micromammal species (A. Martín-Taboada unpubl. data [for the prey species above, the solar PV facilities can act as refuges because hunting by humans is prohibited in this type of facility]); and (3) the increased availability of perches and resting sites compared to the surrounding agricultural lands, where they are typically scarce. Investigating these aspects (i.e., disturbance and food availability) as mechanisms that have a direct effect on raptor communities can provide basic information when considering possible management measures (Smith and Dwyer 2016).

To our knowledge, no studies have been published in peer-reviewed scientific journals on the behavior of raptors inside solar PV facilities. Smith and Dwyer (2016), although they did not study the behavior, examined the raptor community at a solar energy facility and concluded that bird abundance was higher before its construction than during its operation. Most recently, Gerringer et al. (2022) observed Greater Sage-Grouse (Centrocercus urophasianus) resting and feeding inside a solar PV facility. Other researchers have focused their studies on bird communities, but found inconclusive results. DeVault et al. (2014) found that species diversity was higher in control areas than in solar PV facilities, while abundance was more than twice as high within solar PV facilities. In contrast, Visser et al. (2018) found that species’ richness and mean abundance were lower in solar PV facilities than in control areas. For these reasons, we believe that there is insufficient scientific evidence regarding the potential impacts of PV facilities on wildlife.

Conclusions and Limitations. More studies on the interaction between wildlife and solar PV facilities are needed to minimize the cumulative potential impacts of the proliferation of this type of infrastructure. The results of our study on the occurrence and use of raptors at this solar PV facility are significant owing to the observed frequent use, which, at least in our study case, shows the

compatibility between this type of energy production infrastructure and the usual use by raptors. The scarcity of these types of data enhances the significance of our research. Nevertheless, the absence of data on the conditions before the establishment of the solar PV facility or at a control area nearby hinders our ability to precisely determine the true impact of these infrastructures on raptors. Although, as with other energy sources, the impact of solar PV facilities is site- and species-specific (Lovich and Ennen 2011), it is necessary to adopt study approaches that allow us to objectively assess the responses of wildlife (i.e., behavior and space use) to the installation of solar PV facilities. Like other researchers before us (Smith and Dwyer 2016, Visser et al. 2018, Chock, et al. 2020), we recommend using before–after control–impact (BACI) study designs that allow comparison of preconstruction and postconstruction data and provide a robust methodology to identify the effects of solar PV facilities on wildlife. Smith and Dwyer (2016) used a BACI study design to show that raptor abundance declined when a solar energy facility was built, suggesting that raptors avoid the facility. For future research, if preconstruction data are not available, it is advisable to consider control areas near the facility. We recommend that monitoring during the operational phase should be conducted over the operational life of solar PV facilities (i.e., long-term monitoring), because short-term studies do not provide robust indicators of the true impact (Madders and Whitfield 2006, Farfán et al. 2017, 2023).
